newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax reform plan to be delayed to 1997.
newsitem.headline: German tax reform plan to be delayed to 1997.

text.p: The Bonn government, still smarting from an autumn tax row which nearly ripped apart Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party alliance, said on Tuesday that work on drafting a major tax reform would be delayed into 1997.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said coalition parties would talk over the next few days about delinking a plan to cut the unpopular solidarity tax from the broader tax reform debate.
The Free Democrat junior coalition partners are anxious for a decision this year on a cut in the solidarity tax, aimed at helping finance the reconstruction of east Germany.
"We are talking about that," Waigel told reporters after a meeting of his parliamentary faction.
Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), told a news briefing the finishing touches on the tax strategy would be completed by the end of January.
Waigel heads a coalition tax commission made up of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), the CSU and the Free Democrats which had been due to present final proposals before Christmas.
But the policy team has been unable to agree on big cuts in income tax due to take effect in 1999 under a plan to simplify the tax system and lighten the overall burden on Germans.
Glos, a powerful operator on the Bonn political scene, said "too many questions are still open" to wrap up the tax strategy as originally planned at a coalition meeting on December 18.
Leaders say the content of the tax plan is more important than the timetable in drafting a reform which could prove decisive in general elections in 1998.

Bonn also wants to get its sums right to ensure Germany can back up its demands for a tough European stability pact by meeting and sticking to the strict criteria in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union.
Waigel has favoured cutting the lowest income tax bracket to around 20 percent from 26 percent now and slashing the top rate to 40 percent from 53 percent.
But the FDP, whose support has been ebbing away during the 14 years of the Kohl government, has pinned its political survival on more ambitious tax cuts.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle said the FDP still favoured an income tax model with three tax bands at 15, 25 and 35 percent. The FDP has also floated the idea of a 10 percent entry rate -- something that Glos rejected.
The tax commission meets on Wednesday and Westerwelle told German radio he hoped the main points of the tax package would be confirmed, while adding: "Quality comes before speed."

Coalition parties agree on the broad goal of reducing the overall tax burden on Germans by around 30 billion marks ($19.3 billion) -- but will face resistance from interest groups against scrapping tax breaks to compensate for some of the income tax cuts.
Glos said there were still questions open on taxing life insurance policies. Calls by the FDP to introduce elements of the reform in 1998 remain undecided, he added.
Coalition officials have played down comparisons with a row in the autumn over proposals by Kohl's CDU to hike taxes to help cover a shortfall in state revenues.
Kohl at one point threatened to resign before a compromise on delaying a cut in the solidarity tax, raised to finance east German reconstruction, by one year to 1998 was agreed by a reluctant FDP.

The holdup in the government's tax deliberations provided fresh ammunition for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who fought hard to block abolition of wealth taxes in Waigel's 1997 tax bill, to attack government tax plans.
"The coalition should finally end its in-fighting and draft a tax plan which is financially solid and meets the demands of a real reform," SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said. ($1=1.5541 Mark)
